Korrespondenz B (1933  1946)

Briefe, Briefentwürfe, Briefabschriften, Postkarten, Telegramme, Rundbriefe, Notizen, Deklarationen, Ehrenerklärungen ("statements"), Resolutionen, Resolutionsentwürfe, Verträge, Presseerklärungen, Aufstellungen, Rechnungen, Lebensläufe, Internierungslisten und Manuskripte, maschinenschriftlich, handschriftlich und hektografisch aus Argentinien, Australien, Bulgarien, Frankreich, Großbritannien, Hawaii, Kanada, Marokko, Portugal, der Schweiz und den USA von und an u.a.Eva Lewinski (-Pfister), Willi Eichler, Käte Labischin, Hanna Bertholet, Hans Jahn, Erna Blencke, Hans Wistuba, Douglas Lowe, Walter Fliess, Erwin Schoettle, Hans Lehnert, Elisabeth Irmer, Ilse Doberer, Ernst Fröhlich, Otto Lehmann-Russbüldt, Ilse Schultz, Nora Loewi, Herta Gotthelf, George F. Eichler Kriegsziel; W. Eichlers Projekt einer "Zusammenkunft britischer und kontinentaler Sozialisten"; Verhältnis des Freiheitsbundes Deutscher Sozialisten zur Union; Projekt einer Europäischen Föderation; Judenverfolgung in Deutschland; Hilda Olday/Fritz Eberhard; Labour Party und britisches Organisierung einer möglichst raschen und sicheren Kommunikation zwischen der Schweiz und Großbritannien; Probleme der ISK-Emigration in USA beim Aufbau einer funktionierenden Gruppe; Redaktions-, Vertriebs- und schließlich Papierprobleme der neuen ISK-Zeitschrift "Renaissance"; Kriegseintritt der Sowjetunion; Charakter des Krieges; Verhältnis des ISK bzw. der Union zu den Kommunisten; Verwertung der aus der Schweiz von R. Eichlers und anderer, die Internierung von deutschen Antifaschisten in Großbritannien zu verkürzen und aufzuheben: Hilfeersuchen Betroffener, "statements" Angehöriger oder Bekannter, Informationsaustausch zwischen Internierten und Joint Committee for Assistance (JCA), offizielle Korrespondenz zwischen Home Office und JCA; Kontaktaufnahme W. Lehnert und A. Petzold über Nelsons Philosophie; Augenzeugenberichte über die Stimmung der Bevölkerung in Frankreich; Augenzeugenberichte über die Lage in Lissabon; Papiere der "IGB-Kommission zur Beratung von Angelegenheiten betr. illegale Arbeit in Deutschland"; W. Eichlers Kontaktaufnahme mit Henry Hauck; Stellungnahme der in der Union zusammengeschlossenen Organisationen zum Überfall auf die Sowjetunion; Kontroverse zwischen W. Eichler und K. Hiller über die Union, die "Ethik" und damit zusammenhängende Dinge; "Educational Reports" von E. Moore und A. Flanders; "Zirkularschreiben" O. Lehmann-Russbüldts undReaktionen darauf; "Die deutschen Sozialisten und der Friede"  Entwürfe aus der Union; Papier über die "Neugruppierung der deutschen Gewerkschaftsbewegung in Großbritannien"
entries.english:
Correspondence B (1933–1946)

Letters, letter drafts, letter copies, postcards, telegrams, circular letters, notes, declarations, statements of honor (“statements”), resolutions, draft resolutions, contracts, press releases, lists, invoices, curricula vitae, internment lists, and manuscripts, typewritten, handwritten, and mimeographed, from Argentina, Australia, Bulgaria, France, Great Britain, Hawaii, Canada, Morocco, Portugal, Switzerland, and the United States, to and from, among others, Eva Lewinski (-Pfister), Willi Eichler, Käte Labischin, Hanna Bertholet, Hans Jahn, Erna Blencke, Hans Wistuba, Douglas Lowe, Walter Fliess, Erwin Schoettle, Hans Lehnert, Elisabeth Irmer, Ilse Doberer, Ernst Fröhlich, Otto Lehmann-Russbüldt, Ilse Schultz, Nora Loewi, Herta Gotthelf, George F. Green, G. Wallace, Edith Moore, Mary Saran, Hans Gottfurcht, Mohammed Hatta, Edo Fimmen, Wilhelm Heidorn, Klara Deppe, Grete Henry, Harry Richter, Jef Rens, Ludwig Rosenberg, Walther Victor, P. Cromwell, Charlotte Olbrisch, Irmgard Litten, Lotte Leonhard, Gertrud Jelletz, Grace E. Meyette, George Warren, Alida de Jager, W. Bondy, Claud. W. Sykes, Wolf Nelki, Hans Lewinski, Hans Vogel, Erich Ollenhauer, Kurt Doberer, Erich Lewinski, Herta Lewinski, Frieda Timmermann (-Albrecht), Alfred Petzold, Karl Otten, Walter Auerbach, Erich Irmer, Hilda Olday (Hilde Meisel), J. H. Oldenbroek, Lola Mayer, Erna Mros (-Mayer, later -Kakies), Gisela Peiper (-Kühn, later -Konopka), Liselotte Wettig, Charlotte Sonntag, Lola Reitz, Rainer Schmidt, Gustav Heckmann, Nelli Janovski, Anna Beyer, Eugen Albrecht, Fritz Eberhard, F. Demuth, Walter Zundel, Antoine Seilern, Patrick Gordon Walker, Liesel Buckner, Anna Stein, Kurt Hiller, Hans Lehmann, Otto Pfister, Walter Schevenels, René Bertholet, Eugen Brehm, Kurt Labischin, Wilhelm Sander, Henry Hauck, Fritz Gross, Otto Bennemann, Alfred Dannenberg, Jupp Kappius, Gustav Krentler, Paul Walter, Erhardt Konopka, Erna Lange, Jacob Walcher, Max Baruth, Lise Oppenheimer, Hedwig Fliess, Dosio Koffler, Walter Loeb, Paul Fliess, Franziska Bennemann, Hans Maeder, Pierre Krier, Heinrich Bisser, Anna Bisser, Marga Plöger, Rudolf Krautter, Gerhard Gleissberg, Ilse Löwenstamm, K. F. Bieligk, C. A. Smith, Otto Kahn-Freund, Erwin Fischer, Minna Specht, Rhush Rhees, Gerhard Kreyssig, Victor Bodson, J. H. Lothar, Willy Hofmann, Wilfried Israel, Werner Burmeister, Zeko Torboff, Louis Levy, Dores Smets, John Price, Albert Einstein, Sophie Friedländer, Harry Brown, Paul Stamfort, Hans Jaeger, E. J. Gumbel, S. Adler-Rudel, Lilian Fearn, S. Retzlaw, M. Hofmann, P. Treves. They concern, among other things, efforts to bring ISK comrades who had fled to southern France, Algeria, and Morocco to safety; attempts to secure entry to the United States for Hanna and René Bertholet; the situation of socialist émigrés in the United States; the question of war aims and the most effective possible propaganda against fascist Germany; internment in Great Britain and release procedures; conditions in Australian internment camps; editorial and distribution matters concerning “Commentary”; initial contacts and preparations for forming the “Union of German Socialist Organizations in Great Britain”; relations between the ISK and Neu Beginnen; ways of obtaining information from countries under Nazi rule; the forms and extent of participation by the antifascist opposition in Great Britain in the Allies’ war effort; resumption of clandestine work on the continent; the controversy over Vansittart; Edo Fimmen’s failing health; the controversy over W. Eichler’s war aims; W. Eichler’s project for a “meeting of British and continental socialists”; relations between the Freedom League of German Socialists and the Union; a European federation project; persecution of Jews in Germany; Hilda Olday/Fritz Eberhard; the Labour Party and British efforts to organize the quickest and safest possible communications between Switzerland and Great Britain; problems faced by ISK émigrés in the United States in building an effective group; editorial, distribution, and finally paper-supply problems of the new ISK journal “Renaissance”; the Soviet Union’s entry into the war; the character of the war; relations between the ISK or the Union and the Communists; use in publications of the ISK, the ITF (“Fascism”), or the BBC of information from France and Germany transmitted from Switzerland by R. Bertholet; the struggle against Nazi propaganda in Latin America; relations between the Popular Socialists and the Union; problems of ISK work in England; dissatisfaction with W. Eichler’s “Renaissance” in Union circles; René and Hanna Bertholet’s travel plans; interventionism and isolationism in the United States; organizational questions of the French trade-union movement; plans for Germany’s future; financing clandestine work in France; and the end of “Renaissance.” Also included are documents concerning W. Eichler’s and others’ efforts to shorten and end the internment of German antifascists in Great Britain: requests for help from those affected, statements by relatives or acquaintances, exchanges of information between internees and the Joint Committee for Assistance (JCA), and official correspondence between the Home Office and the JCA; W. Eichler’s contact with Jef Rens; documents relating to the “Union of German Socialist Organizations in Great Britain,” including W. Eichler’s report on its beginnings, the joint founding “declaration” of its constituent organizations and drafts, invitations to meetings of its executive committee and working committee, and rules of procedure; the constitution of the “Country Group of German Trade Unionists in Great Britain” and invitations to its working committee; an academic dispute between H. Lehnert and A. Petzold about Nelson’s philosophy; eyewitness reports on public sentiment in France and conditions in Lisbon; papers of the “IFTU Commission for the Consultation of Matters Concerning Clandestine Work in Germany”; W. Eichler’s contact with Henry Hauck; the position of the organizations united in the Union on the attack on the Soviet Union; a dispute between W. Eichler and K. Hiller about the Union, “ethics,” and related matters; “Educational Reports” by E. Moore and A. Flanders; O. Lehmann-Russbüldt’s “circular letter” and reactions to it; drafts from the Union of “The German Socialists and Peace”; and a paper on the “reorganization of the German trade-union movement in Great Britain.”
